questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a foul-smelling right lower extremity soft tissue infection. He was obese and had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, anemia, hyperlipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and a recent deep vein thrombosis. He had no known drug allergies. Home medications were ferrous sulfate 325 mg PO TD, tizanidine 2 mg PO BD, theophylline 300 mg PO BD, warfarin 5 mg PO daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg PO daily. On examination, he was afebrile with an infected ulcer on his right lower leg. Investigations: Total white cell count 9800 cells/mm3 MRI: no evidence of underlying osteomyelitis Wound swab culture: mixed organisms including Pseudomonas isolated Plans were to treat the infection with ciprofloxacin PO and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid PO.
questions.lead_in: What medication would be most likely to interfere with the effectiveness of this planned antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Ferrous sulfate Atorvastatin would not be expected to interact with the planned antibiotic regimen. Ciprofloxacin can significantly increase serum concentrations of theophylline, tizanidine, and warfarin and should be avoided in combination with these agents. Polyvalent metallic cations, such as ferrous sulfate, can adsorb oral fluoroquinolone doses and dramatically reduce systemic exposure and clinical effects of the fluoroquinolone.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q5

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man presented with fever, rigors, neck pain, and respiratory distress. He had had a sore throat for the preceding week. On examination, his heart rate was 148 beats/minute, temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 82/54 mmHg, SaO2 89% on room air. Examination of the oropharynx showed erythema over the soft palate and swollen tonsils. His neck movements were restricted, and there was tenderness and induration over the right jugular vein. Investigations: Peripheral white cell count 28.7 ×109/L (4.0–11.0) Platelets 67 ×109/L (150–400) CXR: multifocal bilateral infiltrates CT neck:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Fusobacterium necrophorum Lemierre’s syndrome is characterized by thrombosis and suppurative thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein. It is associated with disseminated septic emboli to the lungs and other sites. The most common pathogen is Fusobacterium necrophorum, but other organisms implicated include Eikenella, Bacteroides, and streptococcal species. Organisms may be isolated from blood cultures and from infective metastases. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q48

questions.question: A 24yo old male presents with fever, hypotension, worsening respiratory distress. CT shows bilateral opacities (rounded) and a left sided empyema. A week ago, the patient had a sore throat. This has now worsened.

parts.text: List the syndrome and the organism.

cohort_answer.text: ?Invasive GAS/toxic shock syndrome, Streptococcus pyogenes; ?Lemierre's syndrome from Fusobacterium.

questions.question: 14yo female, healthy and no allergies, 1 week of sore throat. Non-productive cough, chest pain, dyspnea, unilateral exudative tonsil. CXR shows bilateral consolidation. BCx grows pleomorphic GNB only in the anaerobic bottle.

parts.text: What is the most common organism?
What test would you do that would confirm your diagnosis and what is the expected finding
What test would you do to rule out a severe complication
For this patient what empiric antibiotic would you choose

questions.model_answer: a) Unifying syndrome: Lemierre syndrome (septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with septic pulmonary emboli, following oropharyngeal infection). b) Most common organism: Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) Confirmatory test: contrast-enhanced CT of the neck; expected finding is thrombosis (filling defect) of the internal jugular vein. d) Test to rule out severe complication: CT chest to assess for septic pulmonary emboli/multiple cavitating nodules (already suggested by bilateral consolidation on CXR). e) Empiric antibiotic: a β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam) or metronidazole combined with a third-generation cephalosporin, given F. necrophorum is frequently penicillin-resistant (beta-lactamase producing).

questions.question: Patient presents with pharyngitis, fever, chest pain, cough, exudative tonsillitis. Chest x-ray shows multifocal airspace disease. Blood cultures are growing pleomorphic GNBs in the anaerobic bottle only.

parts.text: What is the most likely syndrome?
What is the most common organism (genus and species)?
What is one investigation you would do to diagnose the patient, and what do you expect it to show?
What is one investigation you would do to look for complications of the infection, and what do you expect it to show?
What is one empiric treatment regimen?

questions.model_answer: a) Most likely syndrome: Lemierre syndrome. b) Most common organism (genus/species): Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) Investigation to diagnose: contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, expected to show internal jugular vein thrombosis. d) Investigation for complications: CT chest, expected to show septic pulmonary emboli (multiple peripheral, often cavitating nodules). e) Empiric treatment: piperacillin-tazobactam (or metronidazole plus a cephalosporin) - avoid penicillin monotherapy given frequent beta-lactamase-mediated penicillin resistance in F. necrophorum.

questions.question: A young patient presents with a sore throat. There is some purulence noted at the oral mucosa at the back of her mouth/uvula. She now returns and appears sick. Imaging shows a bilateral pneumonia. She is healthy at baseline.

parts.text: c. What is the best test to diagnose and what do you expect to see?
d. What additional test can be done?
e. What treatment/antibiotics do you recommend?

cohort_answer.text: a) Lemierre's syndrome. b) Fusobacterium necrophorum. c) CTA of neck - demonstrating IJV thrombophlebitis. d) Blood cultures. e) Piperacillin-tazobactam (in case beta lactamase) OR CTX + Metronidazole; +/- anticoagulation.

questions.question: 18. A man with an odontogenic infection on amoxicillin. No improvement on therapy.

parts.text: Name 2 typical organisms that would not be covered by amoxicillin therapy alone
Name 2 organisms that would not be covered by metronidazole alone
Why does metronidazole only work for anaerobes.

questions.model_answer:
a) Two organisms not covered by amoxicillin alone: (1) beta-lactamase-producing anaerobes (e.g., Prevotella or Fusobacterium species) (2) Staphylococcus aureus (particularly beta-lactamase-producing or methicillin-resistant strains).
b) Two organisms not covered by metronidazole alone: (1) viridans/anginosus group streptococci (facultative aerobes central to odontogenic infection) (2) Staphylococcus aureus (an aerobe).
c) Metronidazole only works against anaerobes because its nitro group requires intracellular reduction by low-redox-potential, oxygen-independent electron transport proteins (e.g., pyruvate-ferredoxin oxidoreductase/ferredoxin) found only in anaerobic (and some microaerophilic) organisms; this reduction generates cytotoxic free-radical intermediates that damage microbial DNA. Aerobic organisms lack this anaerobic metabolic pathway/redox environment, so the drug is never activated in them.
